findings.claim: The model exists in two separate variants; the W8A16 one you want is qualcomm/Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized (AI Hub id whisper_large_v3_turbo_quantized), and it supports ONLY w8a16 — no float, no TFLite.
findings.detail: Two distinct HF repos and two AI Hub pages: qualcomm/Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo (precision string 'float') and qualcomm/Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized (precision string 'w8a16'). The quantized model's auto-generated evaluate.py declares SUPPORTED_PRECISION_RUNTIMES = {Precision.w8a16: [QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY, PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX, VOICE_AI]} — three runtimes, one precision. There is no TFLite/LiteRT target and no ONNX-with-QNN-EP target other than the PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX wrapper (which still wraps a device-specific context binary). manifest.yaml sets orchestrator_runtimes: [voice_ai], voice_ai_sdk: asr, requires_aot_prepare: true, is_aimet: true, supported_precisions: [w8a16].

findings.claim: KILLER CONSTRAINT: the encoder graph is hard-compiled to a fixed 30-second mel window. Your 0.3–15s segments get zero-padded to 30s and pay the full encoder cost every time.
findings.detail: I pulled the metadata.json out of the actual 8 Gen 3 asset zip. encoder.bin declares exactly one input: input_features, shape [1, 128, 3000], dtype uint16 (quantized, scale 4.746e-5, zero_point 31605). 3000 mel frames = 30.0s at 10ms hop. No dynamic axis. Confirmed in source: qai_hub_models/models/_shared/hf_whisper/model.py has module constants SAMPLE_RATE=16000, CHUNK_LENGTH=30, AUDIO_EMB_LEN=1500, MELS_AUDIO_LEN=AUDIO_EMB_LEN*2, and get_input_spec() hardcodes shape=(1, num_mel_bins, MELS_AUDIO_LEN). The reference app confirms the padding behaviour: chunk_and_resample_audio() returns `[audio]` unmodified when the clip is under 30s (number_of_full_length_audio_chunks == 0), and the HF feature extractor then pads it to 3000 frames. So encoder latency is a constant per commit, independent of segment length.

findings.claim: Real download and on-disk bytes for Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: 820 MB zip, 1.02 GB unpacked (encoder.bin 740 MB + decoder.bin 282 MB). Assets are per-SoC, not portable.
findings.detail: Measured directly via HTTP HEAD and a zip-central-directory range read against the published S3 assets (not from the model card). whisper_large_v3_turbo_quantized-qnn_context_binary-w8a16-qualcomm_snapdragon_8gen3.zip = 859,783,378 bytes (820.0 MiB). Contents: encoder.bin 775,831,552 bytes (739.9 MiB), decoder.bin 295,854,080 bytes (282.1 MiB), metadata.json 16,292 bytes. Unpacked total 1,071,685,632 bytes (1022 MiB). The other two runtimes are the same size (precompiled_qnn_onnx 859,786,903; voice_ai 859,980,169). For scale, the float variant is 2,018,863,741 bytes (1,925 MB). Your current default 'multi' tier is ~190 MB, so this is a ~4.3x download and ~5.4x disk increase — and it is a *second* download, not a replacement.

findings.claim: Published Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 latency (w8a16, QNN context binary): encoder 1340.577 ms, decoder 4.468 ms/token. Qualcomm states encoder time IS time-to-first-token and decoder time is per additional token.
findings.detail: Full 8 Gen 3 rows from the quantized model card — decoder: PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX 4.510 ms (14–27 MB), QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY 4.468 ms (16–24 MB), VOICE_AI 4.514 ms (16–24 MB); encoder: PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX 1421.004 ms (2–13 MB), QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY 1340.577 ms (1–8 MB), VOICE_AI 1356.408 ms (1–8 MB). All NPU. Snapdragon 8 Elite: encoder 1220.377 ms, decoder 3.581 ms (QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY). manifest.yaml description states verbatim: "Time to the first token is the encoder's latency, while time to each additional token is decoder's latency, where we assume a max decoded length specified below." Note the quoted Peak Memory Range (1–8 MB) is activation working set only — it cannot include the ~1 GB of context-binary weights.

findings.claim: Applying those numbers to your VAD segment distribution: every commit costs ~1.34s minimum. Short segments run SLOWER than real time (RTF 2.7 at 0.5s).
findings.detail: Cost model from Qualcomm's own definition: total = 1340.577 ms + 4.468 ms x N_tokens, with the encoder term constant regardless of segment length. At ~150 wpm and ~1.35 tokens/word: 15s segment → ~51 tokens → ~1.57 s (RTF 0.105); 5s → ~17 tokens → ~1.42 s (RTF 0.28); 2s → ~7 tokens → ~1.37 s (RTF 0.69); 0.5s → ~2 tokens → ~1.35 s (RTF 2.70). Because your architecture transcribes per-segment on VAD commit rather than in 30s blocks, you pay the padding tax on every single commit and capture none of the amortisation the 30s design assumes. This is the single fact that decides the tier: against a 'multi' tier the owner already calls "almost instantaneous", a flat ~1.4s per commit is a regression in felt latency even though absolute WER would improve.

findings.claim: LICENSING IS PROBABLY FINE, and much better than expected: the model is labelled Apache-2.0, and even the stricter Qualcomm AI Hub Proprietary License explicitly permits shipping the assets inside a commercial app — while forbidding standalone redistribution.
findings.detail: manifest.yaml declares license_type: apache-2.0 and license: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/v4.42.3/LICENSE. Both AI Hub model pages display 'APACHE-2.0'. The ai-hub-models repo code is BSD-3-Clause. The AI Hub FAQ states models listed as download-now are free to use and that the platform is 'completely free to use' in production, with only some model-maker models being for-purchase. Separately I extracted and decoded the Qualcomm AI Hub Proprietary License PDF (its text is font-cipher-obfuscated; I recovered the plaintext). Section 1 grants a 'non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable, limited royalty-and-fee-free license' to, verbatim, '(iv) distribute and sublicense the Software solely in object code format and as incorporated in Your software application' — followed by 'For the avoidance of doubt, nothing herein grants You a license to distribute or sublicense the Software on a standalone basis.' Section 8 (Indemnity) explicitly contemplates 'Your posting of any software applications on one (1) or more application download websites or stores for end user download.' Practical read: bundling/shipping inside com.whispereverywhere is permitted; serving the raw .bin from your own CDN as a standalone file is the risky pattern, which cuts against your download-on-demand model. Section 2(d) also lists prohibited use cases (none of which you touch) and Section 2(a) forbids reverse-engineering the object code.

findings.claim: The real licensing/shipping problem is NOT the weights — it's the QNN/QAIRT runtime libraries you must bundle in the APK, which are not Apache-2.0.
findings.detail: metadata.json records tool_versions.qairt = 2.45.0.260326154327 and chipset_attributes htp_version 75, soc_model 57. A QNN context binary cannot be executed by whisper.cpp or by ONNX Runtime alone — it requires the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct (QAIRT/QNN) runtime .so set (libQnnHtp.so plus the V75 stub/skel for Hexagon), or the Voice AI ASR SDK, obtained from Qualcomm Package Manager. Those SDK binaries carry their own Qualcomm license, entirely separate from the Apache-2.0 model card, and adding them is a meaningful APK-size and legal-review item on top of the 820 MB model. manifest.yaml's orchestrator_runtimes: [voice_ai] and voice_ai_sdk: asr indicate Voice AI SDK is the intended, supported integration path rather than a raw QNN embed.

findings.claim: Device gating would be extremely narrow: only 12 chipsets have prebuilt assets and only 4 are phone SoCs. Your Z Fold6 is covered (SM8650 is an explicit alias).
findings.detail: release_assets.json lists exactly these chipset slugs: qualcomm-qcm6690, qualcomm-qcs8275, qualcomm-qcs8550-proxy, qualcomm-qcs9075, qualcomm-sa7255p, qualcomm-sa8775p, qualcomm-snapdragon-7gen4, qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-for-galaxy, qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-gen5-for-galaxy, qualcomm-snapdragon-8gen3, qualcomm-snapdragon-x-elite, qualcomm-snapdragon-x2-elite. Only four are mobile phone parts (8gen3, 8-elite-for-galaxy, 8-elite-gen5-for-galaxy, 7gen4); the rest are IoT/automotive/laptop. The extracted metadata.json confirms chipset_attributes.aliases = ['qualcomm-snapdragon-8gen3', 'sm8650'] with reference_device 'Samsung Galaxy S24 (Family)' — so the Z Fold6's SM8650 is directly supported. But each SoC needs its own 820 MB download, and anything outside those four phone SoCs gets nothing.

findings.claim: No WER or accuracy delta for the W8A16 quantization is published anywhere — not on the model card, not on AI Hub, not in the repo.
findings.detail: perf.yaml for whisper_large_v3_turbo_quantized contains zero occurrences of wer/accuracy/psnr. The model card offers only qualitative language ('minor quality degradation' relative to large-v3, 'robust performance in realistic, noisy environments'). The repo ships an evaluate.py harness (DEFAULT_EVAL_DEVICE = 'Samsung Galaxy S25 (Family)') so you could measure it yourself, but Qualcomm publishes no float-vs-w8a16 number. For reference the upstream large-v3-turbo vs large-v3 gap is reported at ~0.39pp average WER, but that is the float baseline and says nothing about the W8A16 step.

findings.claim: ANOMALY worth flagging: Qualcomm's own published numbers show the FLOAT variant's encoder running ~2.9x FASTER than the W8A16 variant on the same 8 Gen 3 (466 ms vs 1341 ms).
findings.detail: qualcomm/Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo (precision column literally 'float') on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: encoder QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY 466.402 ms, decoder 7.961 ms; all NPU. The quantized repo on the same chip: encoder 1340.577 ms, decoder 4.468 ms. The decoder direction is sane (quantized is faster), the encoder direction is inverted. I verified both variants are genuinely full-size and real (float asset is 1,925 MB, quantized 820 MB), so this is not a mislabelled stub. Plausible explanations: fp16 on Hexagon HTP is extremely well optimised and the W8A16 encoder is hitting requant/layout overhead, or the two rows were measured under different graph-partitioning configs. Either way, do not assume 'quantized = faster' here — and note that if the float encoder number is real, the fastest path is a 1.93 GB download, which is worse for your use case, not better.

findings.claim: MUCH more promising alternative found: Whisper-Small-Quantized is an NPU build of essentially the same weights your default 'multi' tier already uses — 280 MB, and a 5x faster encoder (271 ms vs 1341 ms).
findings.detail: qualcomm/Whisper-Small-Quantized, checkpoint openai/whisper-small (the exact multilingual model behind your current default multi tier), w8a16, input 80x3000. Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: encoder QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY 270.846 ms, decoder 6.038 ms/token, NPU. Asset measured by HEAD: whisper_small_quantized-qnn_context_binary-w8a16-qualcomm_snapdragon_8gen3.zip = 293,591,763 bytes (280.0 MiB). Same fixed-30s-window caveat applies, but the constant is 271 ms instead of 1341 ms: a 2s segment costs ~313 ms and a 15s segment ~579 ms. That is a plausible 'faster multi' story on capable hardware rather than a 'bigger, slower, 820 MB' story — and it is the same model family you already validate against, so quality regression risk is near zero.

findings.claim: Architecture detail relevant to your JNI layer: the split is encoder-once / decoder-per-token, with ~14.6 MB of cross-attention KV cache handed from encoder to decoder on every segment.
findings.detail: From the extracted metadata.json: encoder.bin outputs k_cache_cross_0..3 [20,1,64,1500] uint8 and v_cache_cross_0..3 [20,1,1500,64] uint8 — 4 decoder layers x 2 x 1,920,000 bytes = 15,360,000 bytes (14.6 MiB) per segment. decoder.bin takes input_ids [1,1] int32, position_ids [1] int32, attention_mask [1,1,1,200] uint16, the 8 cross caches, and 8 self caches sized [.., 199] — i.e. a strict single-token step loop with a hard 200-token cap (MEAN_DECODE_LEN). Output is logits [1,51866,1,1] uint16 (~104 KB/step). You would be writing the greedy/beam sampling loop, tokenizer, and mel frontend yourself unless you take the Voice AI SDK path. A 200-token cap is fine for 15s segments but is a hard ceiling.

open_questions: Why does the float encoder benchmark at 466 ms while the W8A16 encoder benchmarks at 1341 ms on the same 8 Gen 3? This inverts the expected direction and is the one number that would change the verdict if the 1341 ms figure turns out to be stale or misconfigured. Only an on-device run on the Z Fold6 settles it.

Which license actually governs the precompiled S3 context binaries — the Apache-2.0 shown on the model page, or the Qualcomm AI Hub Proprietary License sitting in the same bucket? The manifest has no deploy_license field and no repo file references the proprietary PDF, so the linkage is unstated. If the proprietary license applies, its 'no standalone distribution' clause conflicts with your download-on-demand model-serving design and you would need to bundle instead. Worth one email to ai-hub-support@qti.qualcomm.com to get it in writing before any engineering spend.

What is the license for the QNN/QAIRT 2.45 runtime .so files (or the Voice AI ASR SDK) that must ship inside the APK to execute the context binary? This is a separate Qualcomm SDK license, is not covered by the model's Apache-2.0 label, and is the actual redistribution risk.

What is the true resident RAM footprint? The published 1–8 MB 'peak memory' clearly excludes the ~1 GB of weights held in the context binary. Whether encoder+decoder can be co-resident, or must be swapped per segment (adding load latency to the 1.34 s), is unanswered and matters a lot on a phone.

Is a shorter-than-30s export actually feasible? The constants (CHUNK_LENGTH=30, AUDIO_EMB_LEN=1500) are forkable and AI Hub supports custom input shapes, but shortening requires slicing Whisper's learned positional embeddings (the whisper.cpp audio_ctx trick) plus a full AIMET re-quantization and per-SoC re-export. Nobody has published accuracy results for that combination, and is_aimet/requires_aot_prepare mean it is not a config flag.
What is the actual W8A16-vs-float WER delta? Unpublished. The repo ships an evaluate.py harness so it is measurable, but it is your measurement to make.
model.bottom_line: The model is real, current (release v0.61.0), and your Z Fold6 is explicitly supported (SM8650 is a listed alias) — and licensing, the thing you flagged as potentially fatal, is very likely NOT the blocker: the assets are labelled Apache-2.0, and even the stricter Qualcomm AI Hub Proprietary License expressly permits distributing them 'as incorporated in Your software application.' What kills it instead is architecture. The encoder is hard-compiled to a fixed 30-second mel window ([1,128,3000], verified from the metadata inside the shipping asset, and from the hardcoded constants in Qualcomm's source), so every one of your 0.3–15s VAD commits pays the identical ~1.34 s encoder cost. That is a flat ~1.4 s per commit against a default tier the owner already calls 'almost instantaneous' — a felt-latency regression, for an 820 MB per-chipset download and 1.02 GB on disk, gated to just four phone SoCs, with no published WER to justify the trade. Two caveats sharpen this: Qualcomm's own numbers oddly show the float encoder 2.9x FASTER than the W8A16 one (466 ms vs 1341 ms), which nobody should trust without an on-device run; and the genuine legal exposure is not the weights but the QNN/QAIRT runtime libraries you would have to bundle, which carry a separate Qualcomm SDK license. My recommendation is to drop Large-V3-Turbo as the candidate tier and evaluate Whisper-Small-Quantized instead: it is an NPU build of openai/whisper-small — the very weights your default multi tier already runs — at 280 MB with a 271 ms encoder, which is a credible 'same quality, 5x faster on capable hardware' story rather than a 'bigger, slower, and a gigabyte' one.

findings.claim: The AI Hub Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized encoder costs ~1.34 s per inference on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and always processes a fixed 30-second window — this is architecturally incompatible with Whisper Everywhere's 0.3–15 s VAD segment pipeline
findings.detail: Qualcomm's published numbers for SM8650: encoder 1340.577 ms (QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY) / 1421.004 ms (PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX) / 1356.408 ms (VOICE_AI); decoder 4.468 ms per token. I confirmed from the model's own metadata.json that the encoder input is a STATIC tensor `input_features [1,128,3000] uint16` — 3000 mel frames = 30 s, hard-compiled into the context binary. There is no `audio_ctx` equivalent: a QNN context binary is compiled for fixed shapes, so the encoder cannot be truncated. Cost per commit in your app: 1-token segment ('yes') = 1345 ms; 25-token segment = 1452 ms; 50 tokens = 1564 ms. Every single VAD commit pays the full ~1.34 s floor regardless of whether the user said one word or fifteen seconds. Your `multi` tier's 'almost instantaneous' feel comes precisely from the audio_ctx=512 optimization (512/1500 ≈ 34% of the encoder window, with quadratic attention savings on top) — the exact lever the NPU path removes. Independent corroboration: the 2026 paper 'NPUsper: Eliminating Redundant Computation for Real-Time Whisper on Mobile NPUs' (arXiv 2607.01108) identifies this precise problem, measures ~1.2 s encoder latency on Snapdragon 8 Elite via QNN/HTP, and states that NPU deployment fundamentally requires static tensor shapes, which traditionally prevents variable-length input.

findings.claim: The model is 1.07 GB on disk and an 860 MB download — PER SoC. I downloaded and measured it.
findings.detail: I pulled both 8 Gen 3 asset bundles. `precompiled_qnn_onnx` zip = 859,786,903 B (859.8 MB); expands to encoder_qairt_context.bin 775,831,552 B (775.8 MB) + decoder_qairt_context.bin 295,854,080 B (295.9 MB) + tiny encoder.onnx (4,658 B) and decoder.onnx (13,863 B) EPContext wrappers + metadata.json. Total on disk 1,071,720,483 B = 1.07 GB. The `qnn_context_binary` bundle is byte-identical in payload (encoder.bin/decoder.bin, same sizes), just without the ONNX wrappers. For scale: this is 4.5x the download and 5.6x the on-disk size of your current default `multi` tier (small q5_1, ~190 MB). Note the AI Hub 'peak memory 1–27 MB' figure refers to inference working set only — the ~1.07 GB of weights is additional resident/mapped memory.

findings.claim: Path (b) LiteRT/TFLite + QNN delegate is not available for this model — AI Hub publishes no .tflite export for Whisper at all anymore
findings.detail: The model's release_assets.json lists exactly three formats across all 12 chipsets: `precompiled_qnn_onnx`, `qnn_context_binary`, `voice_ai`. No `tflite`. I checked Whisper-Small as a counterfactual and it is the same three formats (float precision) — no TFLite either. This is a 2026 shift: qualcomm/ai-hub-apps still ships TFLite Android samples for vision models (image_classification, object_detection, semantic_segmentation, super_resolution via apps/_shared/android/tflite_helpers/), but Whisper has moved to QNN-only. To take the LiteRT path you would have to export and quantize a w8a16 encoder-decoder to TFLite yourself, which is a research project, not an integration.

findings.claim: Qualcomm has NO Whisper Android sample app. Their only first-party Whisper reference is Windows/Python, and it uses ONNX Runtime + QNN EP
findings.detail: I enumerated the full app list in qualcomm/ai-hub-apps: the only Whisper app is `apps/whisper_windows_py`. Android apps present are chatapp_android (Genie), geniex_chat_android, image_classification_android, object_detection_android, semantic_segmentation_android, super_resolution_android — no ASR. The README's 'WhisperKit (Speech to Text) / TensorFlow Lite' row is marked 'Source available on GitHub; not included in the CLI release' and points to argmaxinc/WhisperKitAndroid — a third-party app that was ARCHIVED on 2026-01-24, migrating to `argmax-sdk-kotlin` on Google LiteRT. So the TFLite Android Whisper reference is abandoned. This makes ONNX Runtime + QNN EP the only path with living first-party Whisper reference code, even though that code is Windows Python.

findings.claim: The model provides NO mel spectrogram, NO tokenizer, and NO decode loop — you write all of it, and the reference implementation is greedy-argmax only
findings.detail: From metadata.json, the exact contract. ENCODER: 1 input `input_features [1,128,3000] uint16` QUANTIZED (scale 4.746108970721252e-05, zero_point 31605) — note 128 mel bins, not the 80 used by small/medium; 8 outputs = k/v_cache_cross_0..3, each [20,1,64,1500] and [20,1,1500,64] uint8 = 15.36 MB of cross-KV carried encoder→decoder per segment. DECODER: 19 inputs (input_ids [1,1] int32, position_ids [1] int32, attention_mask [1,1,1,200] uint16 quantized, 4x k_cache_cross + 4x v_cache_cross, 4x k_cache_self_*_in [20,1,64,199] + 4x v_cache_self_*_in [20,1,199,64] uint8); 9 outputs (8 self-cache out + `logits [1,51866,1,1]` uint16 quantized). Self-KV round-trip is 2.04 MB in + 2.04 MB out PER TOKEN. Max decode length is hard-capped at 200 tokens. Qualcomm's whisper_windows_py drives this with HuggingFace `WhisperFeatureExtractor` (mel) + `WhisperTokenizer` (51866-vocab BPE) + a hand-written Python loop doing plain `np.argmax` — no beam search, no temperature fallback, no suppress_blank/suppress_tokens, no compression-ratio or logprob failure detection, no timestamp logic. whisper.cpp gives you all of that for free today; on this path you reimplement it in Kotlin/NDK. One synergy: whisper.cpp already computes 128-bin mel for large-v3, and your retired large-v3-turbo GGML tier carries the same 51866 vocab, so mel + tokenizer could be reused from existing native code.

findings.claim: QNN backend libraries are NOT bundled in the ONNX Runtime AAR and do NOT come from the device /vendor partition — you ship them yourself from Maven Central, ~24 MB per HTP architecture
findings.detail: I downloaded and inspected the AARs. `com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime-android-qnn:1.29.0` (9.0 MB download) contains ONLY jni/arm64-v8a/libonnxruntime.so (23,990,744 B) and libonnxruntime4j_jni.so (111,504 B) — zero Qnn*.so files. The backend comes from `com.qualcomm.qti:qnn-runtime` (Maven Central, latest 2.49.0, 65.9 MB AAR). Minimal runtime set for 8 Gen 3 (HTP v75) with a PRECOMPILED context binary: libQnnHtp.so 2,952,280 + libQnnSystem.so 3,635,672 + libQnnHtpV75Stub.so 727,232 + libQnnHtpV75Skel.so 16,540,228 = 23.86 MB. Crucially, libQnnHtpPrepare.so (87,739,776 B = 87.7 MB!) is only needed for on-device graph compilation and can be excluded when loading precompiled context binaries — a major size saving that depends on choosing the precompiled path. Packaging requires bundling the skel in jniLibs, setting ADSP_LIBRARY_PATH to nativeLibraryDir before the backend loads, and `android:extractNativeLibs="true"` (the DSP loader needs real files on disk) — which conflicts with the modern default of false and inflates install size.

findings.claim: Total APK native-library overhead is ~55 MB for one SoC generation, ~89 MB to cover 8 Gen 3 through 8 Elite Gen 5
findings.detail: Measured, uncompressed arm64-v8a: ORT base (com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime-android:1.26.0) libonnxruntime.so 27,408,600 + libonnxruntime4j_jni.so 111,648 = 27.52 MB; QNN EP plugin (com.qualcomm.qti:onnxruntime-android-qnn:2.5.0) libonnxruntime_providers_qnn.so 4,057,336 = 4.06 MB; QNN v75 backend set 23.86 MB. Total 55.43 MB for HTP v75 only. Adding v79 (16,351,348) and v81 (17,482,732) skels to cover 8 Elite and 8 Elite Gen 5 brings it to 89.27 MB. This sits on top of your existing whisper.cpp JNI lib, and is pure APK growth for a tier most users won't enable.

findings.claim: You must serve a separate ~860 MB model per SoC; only 4 mobile chipsets have prebuilt assets, and 8 Gen 1 / 8 Gen 2 are not among them
findings.detail: release_assets.json v0.61.0 lists 12 chipsets: qcm6690, qcs8275, qcs8550-proxy, qcs9075, sa7255p, sa8775p, snapdragon-7gen4, snapdragon-8-elite-for-galaxy, snapdragon-8-elite-gen5-for-galaxy, snapdragon-8gen3, snapdragon-x-elite, snapdragon-x2-elite. Only four are mobile phone targets: 8gen3, 8-elite-for-galaxy, 8-elite-gen5-for-galaxy, 7gen4. Notably absent for the quantized model: plain 8 Gen 1 and 8 Gen 2 mobile (8gen1 does appear in Whisper-Small float, so this is a per-model gap). At ~860 MB each that is roughly 3.4 GB of CDN assets to host and version. Qualcomm's Flexible Context Binary (FCB) feature can pack multiple SoCs into one deployable EPContext model, but it requires QAIRT 2.48+, is supported only on x86_64 hosts for offline preparation, and AI Hub does not publish FCB assets — you would have to run your own AI Hub compile jobs to produce them.

findings.claim: Concrete version-pinning contract: your Z Fold6 is htp_arch 75 / soc_model 57, and the runtime QNN must be >= the model's build version or loading fails
findings.detail: metadata.json chipset_attributes for the 8 Gen 3 asset: {"aliases":["qualcomm-snapdragon-8gen3","sm8650"], "htp_version":75, "soc_model":57, "reference_device":"Samsung Galaxy S24 (Family)", "supports_fp16":true, "supports_weight_sharing":true}. Galaxy S24 being the reference device is good news for a Fold6 (same SM8650). The model was built with QAIRT 2.45.0.260326154327. Qualcomm's own helper warns: precompiled exports embed a QAIRT version via the EPContext wrapper and 'the installed onnxruntime-qnn's bundled QNN backend must be at least that version to load them — an older bundled backend fails with LoadCachedQnnContextFromBuffer error 5000/1000.' The current validated Android stack is ORT QNN EP 2.5.0 + com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime-android 1.26.0 + com.qualcomm.qti:qnn-runtime 2.49.40, which satisfies >= 2.45. Recommended EP options mirroring AI Hub defaults: enable_htp_fp16_precision=1, htp_performance_mode=burst, htp_graph_finalization_optimization_mode=3, offload_graph_io_quantization=1 (the last one matters — it saves you hand-quantizing the uint16 mel input).

findings.claim: Coexistence with your existing whisper.cpp JNI lib is workable but the binding constraints are real: process memory, env-var ordering, and extractNativeLibs
findings.detail: Symbol collision is unlikely — ORT namespaces its symbols and ggml/whisper.cpp export ggml_*/whisper_*, and they load as separate .so files. The genuine risks are: (1) RAM — 1.07 GB of QNN weights plus a resident whisper.cpp model in a long-lived foreground service; your existing large-v3-turbo GGML tier is already gated at 7 GB RAM, and this would need an equal or stricter gate. (2) ADSP_LIBRARY_PATH must be set before the QNN backend is first loaded (Application.onCreate or JNI_OnLoad), which is easy to get wrong and fails opaquely. (3) android:extractNativeLibs="true" is required for the DSP to load skel files, which increases install footprint and is a global manifest change affecting your whole app, not just this tier. (4) The per-token 2.04 MB in + 2.04 MB out self-KV round-trip means the quoted 4.468 ms/token is a best case measured in AI Hub's harness; without enabling the HTP shared-memory allocator (which needs libcdsprpc.so, sometimes supplied by /vendor) real per-token cost through ORT with CPU-side buffer copies will be worse.

findings.claim: Where the NPU path genuinely wins is long-form batch transcription — about 17x realtime — not live dictation
findings.detail: For a full 30 s window yielding ~100 tokens: 1340.6 ms encoder + 100 x 4.468 ms = 1.79 s to transcribe 30 s of audio ≈ 16.8x realtime, at large-v3-turbo accuracy. That is a genuinely strong number and likely several times faster than small q5_1 on CPU for the same work, with materially better accuracy. The economics invert completely for your live pipeline because the fixed encoder cost is amortized over 30 s of audio instead of being paid fresh on every 0.3–15 s VAD commit. If an NPU tier ships at all, the honest product framing is an offline 'import and transcribe a recording' feature, not a tier above `multi` in the live path.

findings.claim: Path (d) Genie is not applicable to Whisper; the ASR-specific option is the Voice AI SDK, which carries licensing unknowns for a consumer app
findings.detail: Genie is Qualcomm's generative-AI framework for causal LLM token-to-logit inference (used by ai-hub-apps chatapp_android); the ORT QNN docs note Genie backend execution is auto-enabled based on ONNX model contents and requires QAIRT >= 2.45.40 / Genie API >= 1.17 — it is not the encoder-decoder ASR path. The ASR-targeted option is the `voice_ai` export plus the Voice AI ASR SDK, obtained from Qualcomm Package Manager. That SDK would plausibly supply the mel/tokenizer/decode-loop glue you otherwise write yourself, which is its main attraction, but its documentation is oriented to Dragonwing/Ubuntu IoT boards, it is a gated QPM download under the Qualcomm AI Model & Software License rather than a Maven artifact, and I could not verify Android phone support or redistribution rights for a paid Play Store app.

open_questions: Real-device latency through ONNX Runtime on a Z Fold6 — all 1340 ms / 4.47 ms-per-token figures come from Qualcomm's AI Hub profiling harness, not an app. Worth a throwaway spike before any commitment: load the 8 Gen 3 precompiled_qnn_onnx asset via ORT + QNN EP and time one encoder run end to end including mel and buffer copies.

Whether a QNN context binary compiled for one soc_model loads on a different SoC sharing the same HTP arch (e.g. does the 'snapdragon-8-elite-for-galaxy' v79 binary run on a non-Galaxy SM8750?). The existence of the Flexible Context Binary feature implies one binary does NOT span SoCs, but the real granularity — per-arch vs per-soc_model — determines whether you host 3 variants or 4+. Untested.

Whether the Voice AI ASR SDK is licensable and redistributable inside a $4.99 consumer Play Store app, and whether it supports Android phones at all rather than just Dragonwing/IoT boards. If it ships a working mel + tokenizer + decode loop it would remove the largest chunk of custom work on any path.

Actual resident memory with 1.07 GB of context binaries mapped alongside a live whisper.cpp model in a foreground service, and whether Android's low-memory killer tolerates it on 8 GB and 12 GB devices during real use.

Samsung/OEM driver variance: I found no confirmed Samsung-specific QNN defects, but I also found no positive confirmation that a retail One UI Fold6 exposes the HTP to a third-party app with app-bundled skel libraries. Reported failures like ONNX Runtime issue #21214 ('QNN SetupBackend failed Failed to create device. Error: 14001') are unresolved and suggest this is where integration time actually goes.
Install-size impact of flipping android:extractNativeLibs to true app-wide, which is required for the DSP loader but affects your existing whisper.cpp packaging too.
runtime.bottom_line: Recommended path if you build this: ONNX Runtime + QNN Execution Provider consuming AI Hub's `precompiled_qnn_onnx` (EPContext) assets — Maven-only dependencies (com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime-android 1.26.0 + com.qualcomm.qti:onnxruntime-android-qnn 2.5.0 + com.qualcomm.qti:qnn-runtime 2.49.40), no on-device compile so you skip the 87.7 MB libQnnHtpPrepare.so, a clean Kotlin API, and it is the only path with living first-party Qualcomm Whisper reference code (apps/whisper_windows_py). LiteRT/TFLite + QNN delegate is eliminated outright: AI Hub publishes no .tflite for Whisper anymore, and the TFLite Android reference (WhisperKit Android) was archived January 2026. Raw QNN context binaries buy nothing over EPContext but cost you the whole ORT layer. Genie is for LLMs, not encoder-decoder ASR. BUT the product recommendation is: do not ship this as an opt-in tier above `multi` in the live dictation path. The AI Hub model's encoder is hard-compiled to a static [1,128,3000] 30-second window costing ~1.34 s per inference on 8 Gen 3, so every VAD commit in your 0.3–15 s segment architecture pays that full 1.34 s floor — a one-word 'yes' costs 1345 ms. Your `multi` tier feels instantaneous precisely because audio_ctx=512 truncates the encoder, and static NPU shapes remove exactly that lever (independently confirmed by arXiv 2607.01108, which measures 1.2 s on 8 Elite and names this as the core mobile-Whisper problem). The price for that regression is 1.07 GB on disk and an 860 MB download per SoC across 4 mobile chipsets (~3.4 GB hosted), ~55–89 MB of added APK native libs, a hand-written mel + 51866-token BPE tokenizer + greedy decode loop in Kotlin/NDK replacing whisper.cpp's mature decoding heuristics, and a global extractNativeLibs=true manifest change. Where this hardware genuinely wins is long-form batch: ~1.79 s for a full 30 s window ≈ 17x realtime at large-v3-turbo accuracy. If you want the NPU in the product, scope it as an offline "import a recording and transcribe it" feature gated to the four supported SoCs and high RAM — and validate the real end-to-end encoder time on a Fold6 with a throwaway spike before committing engineering to it.

findings.claim: The shippable device set is far narrower than AI Hub's advertised 'supported chipsets' list — prebuilt assets exist only for 8 Gen 3 and newer (plus 7 Gen 4)
findings.detail: The AI Hub model page advertises 21 supported chipsets including Snapdragon 888, 8 Gen 1, and 8 Gen 2. But release_assets.json — the actual prebuilt artifact manifest (v0.61.0) — contains only 12 chipset keys, verbatim: qualcomm-qcm6690, qualcomm-qcs8275, qualcomm-qcs8550-proxy, qualcomm-qcs9075, qualcomm-sa7255p, qualcomm-sa8775p, qualcomm-snapdragon-7gen4, qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-for-galaxy, qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-gen5-for-galaxy, qualcomm-snapdragon-8gen3, qualcomm-snapdragon-x-elite, qualcomm-snapdragon-x2-elite. Snapdragon 888, 8 Gen 1, and 8 Gen 2 are absent. 'Supported chipset' on AI Hub means 'we can run a compile/profile job for it', NOT 'a downloadable binary exists'. Whisper-Small-Quantized has the identical 12-key asset set. Three artifact types per chipset: precompiled_qnn_onnx, qnn_context_binary, voice_ai.

findings.claim: THE DECISIVE NUMBER: the W8A16 turbo encoder costs 1421 ms per inference on the Fold6's SoC — only ~1.4x faster than the CPU tier we already ship
findings.detail: Qualcomm's own published figures, PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX / w8a16 / NPU: Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 encoder 1421.004 ms, decoder 4.51 ms/token; 8 Elite encoder 1232.326 ms, decoder 3.626 ms; 8 Elite Gen 5 encoder 1167.227 ms, decoder 3.295 ms; 8 Gen 1 encoder 1527.758 ms. A typical segment (~40 tokens) on 8 Gen 3 = 1.42 s + 0.18 s ≈ 1.6 s. Our own Fold6 ground truth from the 3.6.0 device session (memory whisper-everywhere-360-local-speed, 2026-08-20): multi (small q5_1, CPU, audio_ctx floor 512) F ≈ 2.3 s, rtf8s 0.41–0.48. So the 809M NPU tier buys ~1.4x on latency — for a ~1 GB download and a ~5% fleet. The accuracy gain (large-v3-turbo vs small) is real; the speed gain is not the step-change the 'massive compute on the table' framing implies.

findings.claim: Whisper-Small-Quantized on the same NPU, same device gate, is 5x faster than the turbo and ~4x faster than the CPU tier it would replace — this is the tier worth building
findings.detail: Whisper-Small-Quantized (w8a16, PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX, NPU): 8 Gen 3 encoder 270.196 ms / decoder 6.176 ms; 8 Elite encoder 222.951 ms / decoder 4.663 ms; 8 Elite Gen 5 encoder 185.642 ms / decoder 3.938 ms; 8 Gen 1 encoder 361.383 ms / decoder 10.39 ms. Per segment on 8 Gen 3: ~0.37 s (short) to ~0.73 s (15 s segment) versus multi CPU's 2.3–3.4 s — a 4–6x win at IDENTICAL model quality (small is exactly what `multi` is today), at ~250–300 MB instead of ~1 GB, behind the same device gate (identical 12-key asset manifest). This also matches what our own 3.6.0 analysis already concluded: the recorded 4.0-scale ticket is 'ORT+QNN PoC with Qualcomm AI Hub Whisper-Small-En on Fold6'.

findings.claim: Qualcomm's own numbers say the W8A16 turbo encoder is 3x SLOWER than the float turbo encoder on the same chip — an anomaly that must be measured before any decision
findings.detail: Same encoder architecture, same chip, two Qualcomm model cards: float Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo on 8 Gen 3 = 471.256 ms encoder / 8.093 ms decoder (peak mem 63–72 MB / 42–55 MB); w8a16 Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized on 8 Gen 3 = 1421.004 ms encoder / 4.51 ms decoder. The float path is also faster on 8 Elite (410.654 vs 1232.326) and 8 Elite Gen 5 (278.258 vs 1167.227). Quantization making a conv-heavy encoder 3x slower is not normal — plausible causes are 16-bit activation paths spilling HTP tensor memory, or an op falling off the NPU. If the float number holds on-device, float turbo at ~0.7 s/segment is the genuinely interesting configuration — but float weights are ~1.6 GB, versus ~809 MB for w8a16. Do not plan around either number until one Fold6 run confirms it.

findings.claim: The fixed 30 s encoder window destroys our single best latency lever — but a custom AI Hub export can restore it
findings.detail: Both AI Hub Whisper models are compiled at input resolution 128x3000 = exactly 30 s of audio, max decoded sequence 200 tokens. A compiled QNN context binary has a FIXED shape: a 0.5 s segment pays the identical 1421 ms as a 15 s one. Our whisper.cpp path does the opposite — `params.audio_ctx = neededFrames` floored at 512 (production default `g_audio_ctx_floor`, lowered 768→512 in 3.6.0 task G4), which the device session measured as multi F 3.5→2.3 s (-35%) and pro-GPU 0.96→0.77 s. Our app segments at 0.3–15 s, so we live almost entirely in the region where the floor is the win. ESCAPE HATCH: qai-hub-models supports export with custom configurations, and the only thing preventing the Whisper encoder from accepting shorter audio is the positional embeddings — so a 10 s-context (128x1000) variant is compilable per chipset via submit_compile_job. That is the highest-leverage engineering move if we go NPU at all, and it would cut the encoder roughly 3x.

findings.claim: AI Hub's 'peak memory' column excludes the model weights — do not use it as a RAM requirement
findings.detail: The quantized turbo encoder reports peak memory of 2–13 MB on 8 Gen 3. A 635M-parameter encoder cannot execute in 13 MB. AI Hub's peak memory is a process-RSS delta during inference; the context-binary weights are mapped/DMA'd to the HTP outside that measurement. Realistic working set, inferred from parameter counts: Whisper-large-v3-turbo is 809M params (32-layer encoder ~635M + 4-layer decoder ~174M, pruned from large-v3's 1550M). At W8A16 that is ~809 MB of weights, giving ~1.0–1.4 GB resident with activations, the ORT session, and the QNN context. Whisper-small (244M) at w8a16 is ~244 MB of weights, ~350–450 MB resident — comparable to the 190 MB GGML footprint we already ship. Gate on ActivityManager.MemoryInfo.totalMem and !isLowRamDevice(), and ensure the whisper.cpp context is torn down before the QNN session loads, never held concurrently.

findings.claim: Recommended runtime detection ladder: five rungs, gating on HTP architecture rather than marketing name
findings.detail: R0 (free, no native code): Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31 — SOC_MODEL/SOC_MANUFACTURER do not exist below API 31; Build.SOC_MANUFACTURER must be Qualcomm/QTI, and UNKNOWN must deny rather than allow (OEM reporting is inconsistent). R1: map Build.SOC_MODEL to HTP arch — SM8450 (8 Gen 1) v69, SM8550 (8 Gen 2) v73, SM8650 (8 Gen 3) v75, SM8750 (8 Elite) v79, SM8850 (8 Elite Gen 5) v81 [v81 unverified]. Gate on the ARCH, not the SKU: the Fold6 is SM8650-AC ('8 Gen 3 for Galaxy') and the asset key is `qualcomm-snapdragon-8gen3` — same v75, so it loads. R2: asset availability — QNN context binaries are NOT portable across HTP arch versions or SDK versions (failure mode: QNN_COMMON_ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_BINARIES), so require a downloaded binary matching this exact arch; there is no on-device recompile path. R3: memory gate (see RAM finding). R4: guarded runtime probe — dlopen + ORT session creation, which is where unsupported silicon actually fails. Runtime is onnxruntime-android-qnn on Maven Central (com.microsoft.onnxruntime, latest 1.27.0; the 1.21.0 AAR is ~7 MB) and the QNN .so dependencies must ship inside the APK.

findings.claim: Failure on unsupported devices is usually a graceful error return, but native crashes are documented — the GpuPolicy sentinel pattern must be carried over, extended to three phases
findings.detail: Documented QNN failure modes are recoverable errors surfaced as exceptions: 'No Snapdragon SOC detected' with failure to create backend_handle on unrecognized soc_id (executorch #16465, CQ8750S soc_id=705); 'QNN SetupBackend failed ... InitializeBackend Failed to initialize backend' (onnxruntime #20124); QNN_DEVICE_ERROR_INVALID_CONFIG (14001) on incompatible hardware; QNN_COMMON_ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_BINARIES across SDK/arch mismatch. But native memory-allocation failures inside the HTP backend are also reported (onnxruntime #22288), so process death is possible. Our existing GpuPolicy already implements exactly the right shape — commit()-to-disk before each risky-first native call, cleared in a finally, stale flag on next launch = permanent per-(versionCode, model) latch. Port it with THREE phases instead of two, because QNN clusters failures differently than OpenCL: (1) backend init / session creation (context-binary deserialize), (2) first encode, (3) first decode. Key the latch on (versionCode, model, htpArch, socModel). Mirror `onCanaryUnavailable` verbatim — the C5b fix that clears canaryPending AND gpuActiveInProcess without touching any permanent flag when no verdict was possible.

findings.claim: The NPU canary MUST carry a speed term — our own GPU canary already proved a correctness-only gate latches ALLOW on a pathologically slow backend
findings.detail: This is the strongest design lesson we already own. GpuCanaryPolicy is correctness-only by construction (empty / <4 of 5 digit positions / >20 token runaway). The 2026-08-20 Fold6 session then measured GPU-VERDICT: BAN reason=slower for multi — rtf8s 0.41–0.48 CPU versus 3.48–3.84 GPU with wer 0.000. The corruption the canary was built to catch did not reproduce; the backend was correct but 9x slower, and a correctness-only canary would have latched ALLOW. The memory records this as an open Decision Gate 2 follow-up ('pull the Settings row or add a speed term to the canary'). Proposed NPU canary: reuse the already-bundled assets/canary_digits.wav (owner re-record, 'one two three four five' @ 2.56 s, commit 5484e3d); reuse GpuCanaryPolicy.canaryPasses verbatim for the correctness term (it is pure and JVM-pinned); add (a) a warm-run wall-clock term that must beat the incumbent CPU tier's measured F on the same clip by a real margin — with multi at 2.3 s on Fold6, require warm ≤ ~1.4 s to latch ALLOW — and (b) a separate cold-load budget (context-binary deserialize can take seconds; cap it, e.g. ≤ 8 s, and hide it behind prewarm). Run the clip twice to separate cold from steady-state. Bonus property: because the encoder is fixed at 30 s, ONE canary latency number predicts every segment length — unlike CPU, where cost varies with duration.

findings.claim: Set disable_cpu_ep_fallback — otherwise ORT silently runs the encoder on CPU and we ship a 'NPU tier' slower than what we have
findings.detail: ORT's QNN EP defaults to falling back unsupported operators to CPU execution. For a 635M-param encoder, partial placement means most of the graph runs on the ARM CPU through ONNX Runtime — which will be substantially slower than our hand-tuned whisper.cpp path with dotprod/i8mm and audio_ctx=512, while the app reports 'NPU'. The QNN EP exposes session.disable_cpu_ep_fallback to raise an exception instead when the model cannot run entirely on the HTP backend. Set it, and treat the exception as a clean deny. This is the software analogue of the same trap the GPU canary fell into: a path that works but is slower, presented as an upgrade.

findings.claim: Roughly 4–6% of the global Android active base can run this — and the gate is anti-correlated with our actual user base
findings.detail: Chain of best-available evidence: Counterpoint puts the premium (≥$600 wholesale ASP) segment at a record 29% of global smartphone sales units in H1 2026, with Apple taking 65% of premium — leaving Android premium at roughly 10% of global units. Within Android premium, Snapdragon 8-series competes with Dimensity 9000-series, Exynos 2x00 and Tensor; Qualcomm's total smartphone SoC share across ALL tiers is 22–24% in H1 2026 (down from 26–27%). Netting out, Snapdragon 8-series flagships are on the order of 5% of annual global units; the shippable cohort is narrower still (8 Gen 3 and newer = 2024 onward, since 8 Gen 1/8 Gen 2 have no prebuilt asset). Against a ~3B Android active base that is roughly 4–6%. US Android skews far higher (~15–25%, Galaxy S/Z ship Snapdragon in the US; Pixel/Tensor is excluded entirely). THE STRATEGIC PROBLEM: the owner's stated base is 'most of the customers are OUTSIDE the US' needing multilingual, and emerging markets skew hard to mid-range MediaTek and Snapdragon 6/7-series — capable share there is plausibly 1–3%. The users who most need multi to get faster are the least likely to pass the gate. A $4.99 paid app does skew premium, which may lift the in-app rate 2–4x over the global figure, but the direction of the mismatch stands.

findings.claim: There is no cross-vendor story — this is Snapdragon-only, and Android's unified path is dead
findings.detail: NNAPI, the one vendor-neutral accelerator API, was deprecated in Android 15; Google's migration guide points developers to TFLite in Play Services or AICore (Gemini Nano) instead. The NN HAL still exists for vendor drivers, but there is no third-party unified NPU API to target. MediaTek: NeuroPilot is real and the LiteRT NeuroPilot Accelerator (successor to the TFLite NeuroPilot delegate) targets Dimensity 7300/8300/9000/9200/9300/9400 — but the published work is LLM/Gemma-oriented and there is no MediaTek-published Whisper NPU model equivalent to AI Hub's; MediaTek's own Genio community thread on Whisper is a question, not a shipping model. Samsung Exynos: ENN SDK is not publicly distributed the way AI Hub is, no public Whisper. Google Tensor: no public NPU execution provider for third-party apps — the EdgeTPU is effectively first-party. Net: each vendor would be a separate port with separate model conversion and separate canaries, not a config flag. Budget the NPU work as Snapdragon-only and permanent.

findings.claim: HTP architecture mapping for the detection allowlist
findings.detail: SM8450 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 1) → HTP v69; SM8475 (8+ Gen 1) → v69; SM8550 (8 Gen 2) → v73; SM8635 (8s Gen 3) → v73; SM8650 (8 Gen 3, incl. SM8650-AC 'for Galaxy' = our Fold6) → v75; SM8750 (8 Elite) → v79; SM8850 (8 Elite Gen 5) → v81 [this last one is inferred from the sequence, not confirmed by a primary source — verify before shipping the allowlist]. Cross-check: AI Hub added an htp-supports-weight-sharing attribute for devices at v73 and above, retrievable via hub.get_devices(); LiteRT's Qualcomm page independently lists SM8850/SM8750/SM8650/SM8550/SM8475/SM8450 as its supported NPU set, which is a useful second source for the SOC_MODEL strings. Practical allowlist for us given the asset manifest: v75 and above only, plus Snapdragon 7 Gen 4.

open_questions: Why is the w8a16 turbo encoder (1421 ms) 3x SLOWER than the float turbo encoder (471 ms) on the same 8 Gen 3? Both are Qualcomm-published. This single number decides whether the tier is worth anything, and it needs one Fold6 measurement before any planning. If float is genuinely 471 ms, the whole recommendation may flip toward float turbo despite ~1.6 GB weights.

Actual download size per chipset ZIP — the S3 asset bucket returns 403 on HEAD, so ~809 MB (turbo w8a16) and ~250-300 MB (small w8a16) are parameter-count inferences, not measured. Needs an authenticated AI Hub account or a real GET to confirm. This is a hard gate for a $4.99 app whose current largest download is 190 MB.
Is HTP v81 correct for SM8850 (8 Elite Gen 5)? Inferred from the version sequence, not confirmed by a primary Qualcomm source. Must be verified before it goes in a shipping allowlist.

Does a context binary built for `qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-for-galaxy` (SM8750-AB) load on a plain SM8750? Theory says yes — binaries are keyed to HTP arch (both v79) — but Qualcomm ships separate 'for Galaxy' assets, which may imply a real difference. Needs one non-Galaxy 8 Elite device to confirm, or we gate 'for Galaxy' assets to Samsung only and lose the rest of the v79 fleet.

Can we actually compile a short-context (e.g. 128x1000 / 10 s) Whisper encoder through qai-hub-models submit_compile_job, and does the positional-embedding change survive w8a16 quantization without accuracy loss? This is the single highest-leverage move and it is entirely unvalidated. It also requires an AI Hub account and a per-chipset compile pipeline in our release process.

What is sustained NPU throughput under thermal load? All AI Hub figures are single cold runs. Our app runs continuous dictation, and the 3.6.0 C8 bench already needed a thermal protocol. A canary that runs cold may over-promise; we likely need a session-scoped soft demotion separate from the permanent latch.

Does the Voice AI SDK path (the third artifact type, `voice_ai`, present for every chipset) offer a better-integrated or faster route than PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX? It is undocumented in what I could reach and is distributed via Qualcomm Package Manager rather than Maven — licensing and redistribution terms unknown.

What is the actual SoC mix of our existing paying install base? Every fleet number here is global-market inference. We ship zero-SDK tracking by decision, so we may have no way to answer this — but if any Play Console device breakdown exists, it beats all of the above and should be checked first.
gating.bottom_line:
The device gate is a solved engineering problem and I can specify it precisely — but the owner has picked the wrong model, and the honest recommendation is to change the target before building anything.

Three findings drive that. (1) The device set is much narrower than advertised: AI Hub lists 21 supported chipsets, but the actual prebuilt asset manifest covers only 8 Gen 3, 8 Elite, 8 Elite Gen 5 and 7 Gen 4 — no 8 Gen 2, no 8 Gen 1, no 888. That is roughly 4-6% of the global Android active base, and it is anti-correlated with our user base: the owner's own stated majority is outside the US on mid-range silicon, and they are the ones who need `multi` to get faster. (2) The turbo's headline number is disappointing on our architecture: 1421 ms encoder on the Fold6's chip, fixed per 30 s window regardless of segment length, versus the 2.3 s we already measured for multi on CPU. That is ~1.4x, for a ~1 GB download. The fixed window is the specific problem — it defeats our audio_ctx=512 floor, which is the lever that bought us 35% in 3.6.0. (3) Whisper-Small-Quantized, on the identical device gate and the identical asset manifest, runs its encoder in 270 ms on the same chip — 4-6x faster than the CPU tier it would replace, at the same model quality, at a quarter of the download. That is the tier worth building, and it is what our own 3.6.0 notes already pointed at ("ORT+QNN PoC with Whisper-Small-En on Fold6").

One anomaly could overturn this and should be measured first: Qualcomm's own cards say the FLOAT turbo encoder is 471 ms — 3x faster than its own w8a16 version. Nobody should plan around either number until one Fold6 run adjudicates it.

On the canary, we already own the most important lesson and should not have to learn it twice. GpuCanaryPolicy is correctness-only, and the 2026-08-20 device session then returned GPU-VERDICT: BAN reason=slower — wer 0.000, 9x slower. A correctness-only canary would have latched ALLOW on that. So the NPU canary must carry a speed term (reuse canary_digits.wav and canaryPasses for correctness; add a warm-run threshold that must beat the incumbent CPU tier's measured F, with cold context-binary load budgeted separately), and the ORT session must set disable_cpu_ep_fallback so silent CPU placement fails loudly rather than shipping as a fake NPU tier. The GpuPolicy crash-sentinel machinery ports over almost unchanged — extended to three phases (session init, first encode, first decode) and keyed on (versionCode, model, htpArch, socModel), since QNN backend init can die natively and context binaries are not portable across HTP versions.

Suggested sequence: PoC Whisper-Small-Quantized on the Fold6 and measure the float-vs-quantized encoder anomaly in the same session — one phone session answers both. Treat large-v3-turbo as an accuracy tier to consider only after the short-context custom export is proven, not as the entry point.

findings.claim: Turbo on 8 Gen 3 NPU is ~3x faster than our current CPU path, but the win is bounded by a FIXED 466ms encoder paid on every segment regardless of length
findings.detail: Qualcomm's published 8 Gen 3 rows (QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY): encoder 466.402 ms, decoder 7.961 ms/token, NPU, peak mem 33-41 MB (decoder) / 1-8 MB (encoder). Input is fixed at 128x3000 = 30 seconds of mel, max 200 decoded tokens. Derived per-segment: 20 tokens = ~626 ms; 45 tokens = ~825 ms; pathological 200 tokens = ~2059 ms. Against our ~2300 ms fixed CPU cost that is 2.8-3.7x faster, and even the worst case beats today. BUT because the encoder input is a fixed 30s window, a 0.3s 'yes' costs the same 466 ms encoder as a 15s sentence. Our architecture commits 0.3-15s segments, so we would pay the full encoder on every commit. The floor for turbo on this SoC is 466 ms/segment and cannot go lower.

findings.claim: THE BURIED LEAD: moving our EXISTING small model to the NPU is an ~8x latency win at zero accuracy risk — a bigger, cheaper win than adding the turbo tier
findings.detail: Qualcomm publishes the same benchmark for whisper-small (multilingual, same checkpoint family as our 'multi' tier) on 8 Gen 3 NPU: encoder 97.324 ms, decoder 9.918 ms/token. A 20-token segment = ~296 ms vs our ~2300 ms CPU = 7.8x faster. Same model, same weights family, identical WER, no new download-size surface, no new language-regression surface. Turbo's encoder costs 4.8x more than small's (466 vs 97 ms) because turbo keeps the full large-v3 encoder (32 layers, d=1280, 128 mel bins) and only prunes the decoder to 4 layers. Note turbo's decoder is actually slightly FASTER per token than small's (7.96 vs 9.92 ms). This means these are two separable decisions, and the cheap high-certainty one is currently being skipped in favor of the expensive uncertain one.

findings.claim: The W8A16 quantized variant the owner wants to evaluate has NO published benchmarks on ANY chipset — every number above is for the FLOAT variant
findings.detail: aihub.qualcomm.com/models/whisper_large_v3_turbo_quantized, /mobile/models/..., and /compute/models/... all return 'This model is currently not supported on any [Mobile/Compute/All Models] chipset.' The pages confirm 'Quantization applied: w8a16' but publish zero latency, memory, or accuracy data. All working 8 Gen 3 numbers come from the separate float model qualcomm/Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo. Qualcomm publishes no WER for either variant. So the premise of the evaluation ('W8A16 QNN/Hexagon') currently has no vendor performance data behind it at all, and the W8A16 accuracy cost on top of turbo's own degradation is entirely unmeasured. Its 'unsupported everywhere' status may also indicate an abandoned or pre-release asset.

findings.claim: The accuracy case is real and it is the ONLY case: turbo roughly halves multilingual error vs small
findings.detail: FLEURS test split, 50 utterances/language, M3 + MLX fp16, July 2026 (third-party, vocova). WER small -> large-v3-turbo: Spanish 6.5->3.3 (-49%), French 14.3->6.7 (-53%), German 12.8->6.0 (-53%), Italian 8.2->3.9 (-52%), Portuguese 11.0->7.2 (-35%), Korean 21.7->14.5 (-33%), Hindi 42.4->22.3 (-47%), Arabic-Egypt 32.7->16.1 (-51%), English 6.6->4.7 (-29%). CER: Japanese 16.4->5.8 (-65%), Mandarin 19.5->8.0 (-59%). Median ~50% error reduction. Corroborated directionally by OpenAI's own turbo release note (turbo performs similarly to large-v2). Caveat: small sample, clean read speech = ceiling conditions, not our noisy dictation reality. Since our multi tier is already perceived as 'almost instantaneous', speed is merely a non-regression requirement — the tier must be sold on accuracy.

findings.claim: Cantonese is a hard carve-out: turbo is catastrophically worse than large-v3 and must not be in the tier's advertised languages
findings.detail: Same FLEURS benchmark: Cantonese CER large-v3 10.5% vs large-v3-turbo 43.3% — a 4x regression, and whisper small does not support it at all. OpenAI's own turbo announcement independently flags 'larger degradation on some languages like Thai and Cantonese'. Also load-bearing for our listing copy: turbo was fine-tuned excluding translation data, so it is NOT usable for speech-to-English translation — if any current or planned feature does translation, turbo cannot back it.

findings.claim: Power strongly favors NPU, but the naive fixed-window drop-in sits at the EXPENSIVE end of the measured range
findings.detail: NPUsper (arXiv 2607.01108, Jul 2026), Monsoon high-voltage power monitor on Galaxy S25 at 5 kHz: their optimized NPU path draws 0.46 W avg / 0.92 J per inference, vs baselines at 2.94-4.05 W / 6.13-13.95 J. NPU vs GPU: 3x faster with power down from 1.99 W to 1.14 W. Crucially their whole thesis is that eliminating 30-second padding is where the savings come from — they measure padded-to-30s encoder at ~720 ms, 3.8x higher than unpadded. Qualcomm's AI Hub turbo model IS the fixed 30s-padded design, so a drop-in inherits exactly the inefficiency the paper attacks. Caveat: measured on whisper base/small on 8 Elite, baselines are streaming systems not our per-segment batch. Qualcomm separately claims 8 Gen 3 Hexagon delivers 40% better perf/W for sustained inference vs 8 Gen 2.

findings.claim: whisper.cpp will never get us here: no Hexagon/QNN backend exists, and the official ggml-hexagon backend structurally cannot run a Whisper encoder
findings.detail: whisper.cpp's backend list (CPU, Metal, CUDA, Vulkan, OpenVINO, CoreML, CANN/Ascend, SYCL, BLAS, ROCm, MUSA, AMD Ryzen AI via VitisAI) contains no Qualcomm entry, including in 1.9.3 (Aug 2026). The official ggml-hexagon backend landed in llama.cpp PR #16547 (merged 22 Oct 2025, authored by Qualcomm engineers Rajdeep Ganguly and Todor Boinovski) supporting Hexagon v73/v75/v79/v81 — but its op set is MUL_MAT/MUL_MAT_ID, ADD/SUB/MUL, RMS_NORM, ROPE, GLU/SWIGLU, SOFTMAX. There are NO convolution ops, and whisper.cpp's encoder is built on ggml_conv_1d_ph + GELU. It is LLM-shaped, self-described as 'experimental and may exhibit instability', and targets llama.cpp. The earlier community PR #12326 (which did touch whisper.cpp) was never accepted upstream. CONCLUSION: retiring GGML turbo on CPU remains correct, and there is no near-term whisper.cpp path to NPU turbo — any NPU tier means a SECOND, parallel inference stack (QNN/ONNX-RT) alongside our existing JNI.

findings.claim: Deployment tax is per-SoC binaries: QNN context binaries are Hexagon-arch-specific and not forward compatible
findings.detail: QNN context binaries are OS-agnostic but device-specific and NPU-only. Hexagon generations map v73 = 8 Gen 2, v75 = 8 Gen 3, v79 = 8 Elite; loading a v75-compiled binary on a v73 device fails outright. Qualcomm's release_assets.json for turbo ships 13 chipset targets (QCS8275, QCS8550-proxy, QCS9075, SA7255p, SA8295p, SA8775p, SD 8 Gen1, 8 Gen3, 8 Elite, 8 Elite Gen5, X Elite, X2 Elite) across three runtimes (precompiled_qnn_onnx, qnn_context_binary, voice_ai), built with QAIRt 2.45.0. Our download-on-demand CDN would need a per-SoC asset matrix plus a capability probe and silent fallback. The tier lights up on Qualcomm only — never on Tensor or Dimensity.

findings.claim: Download size is the most likely deal-breaker and Qualcomm does not publish it
findings.detail: The turbo model card omits model size and parameter count entirely, and release_assets.json carries URLs but no byte sizes. For scale, Qualcomm DOES publish whisper-small float sizes: encoder 391 MB (102M params) + decoder 533 MB (139M params) = 924 MB — versus our 190 MB small q5_1 GGML, i.e. ~5x. Turbo is 809M params; W8A16 weights alone imply roughly 800 MB-1 GB. For a $4.99 app with on-demand model download, a ~1 GB tier asset is a materially different product decision than a 190 MB one. This number is unpublished and must be obtained by actually downloading the 8 Gen 3 assets.

findings.claim: Integration is greenfield: no official Qualcomm Android ASR sample, and the compiled assets carry a separate proprietary license
findings.detail: qualcomm/ai-hub-apps ships Android samples for ChatApp (Genie), GenieX Chat, and TFLite vision models (classification, detection, segmentation, super-resolution) — no ASR/Whisper Android app. The turbo card points to the 'Qualcomm Voice AI SDK' via Qualcomm Package Manager. Licensing is layered: AI Hub Models code BSD-3 and OpenAI checkpoints MIT/Apache-2.0, but the compiled .tflite/QNN assets and QNN libraries fall under the separate 'Qualcomm AI Model & Software License' — needs a legal read before shipping in a paid app. The obvious third-party shortcut is also gone: argmaxinc/WhisperKitAndroid was ARCHIVED in Jan 2026, replaced by the commercial Argmax Pro SDK (LiteRT-based, sales-gated).

findings.claim: Thermals are the weakest-evidenced area and nobody has published what we actually need
findings.detail: No published sustained-dictation thermal data exists for Whisper on Hexagon on 8 Gen 3. General findings only: mobile SoC governors inflate CPU latency 1.3-2.1x past the thermal design point under sustained load (invisible in short-burst benchmarks like Qualcomm's), and heavy sustained generation throttles 30-50% after 15-20 minutes. The directional argument favors NPU — lower watts means less heat, and offloading inference frees the CPU for our 31.25 Hz audio pipeline plus Silero VAD, which currently contend with inference. But note Qualcomm's 466 ms figure is a burst benchmark and carries no throttle allowance. This must be measured on the Fold6 with a 10+ minute continuous dictation run, not inferred.

open_questions: What is the ACTUAL on-disk size of the 8 Gen 3 QNN context binaries for turbo (encoder + decoder)? Unpublished by Qualcomm — must download from release_assets.json and measure. This single number likely decides the whole thing: ~1 GB behaves very differently from ~400 MB for a $4.99 app with on-demand downloads.

Is the W8A16 quantized variant actually alive? Its mobile, compute, and all-models pages ALL say 'not supported on any chipset'. Is it pre-release, deprecated, or broken? Needs a direct question to Qualcomm developer support before building a plan on it.

What is W8A16's WER cost on top of turbo's own degradation? Qualcomm publishes no accuracy data for either variant. Requires our own FLEURS/Common Voice eval on-device across our top 5 shipped languages.

Does the 'Qualcomm AI Model & Software License' permit redistribution of compiled QNN assets inside a paid closed-source app? Distinct from the BSD-3 AI Hub Models code and the MIT/Apache checkpoints. Needs a legal read.

How does turbo-on-NPU behave thermally over 10+ minutes of continuous dictation on the Fold6, and does the 466 ms encoder hold or degrade under throttle? No published data; must be measured with our own harness.

What is our REAL token-count distribution per committed segment? All latency math above is parameterized on assumed 20/45 tokens. Our own telemetry would convert these estimates into actual expected per-segment latency.

Voice AI SDK vs ONNX Runtime QNN EP vs raw QNN context binary — which integration path, given we need a capability probe, graceful fallback, and a per-SoC asset matrix? Each has different runtime .so payload cost added to the APK.

Would a shorter fixed encoder window (e.g. a 10s-input recompile via AI Hub's compile service) be possible? That would attack the 466 ms floor directly, and NPUsper's data suggests it is where most of the waste lives. Unknown whether AI Hub exposes that knob for this model.
baseline.bottom_line: Turbo-on-NPU genuinely beats what we ship on BOTH axes — roughly half the multilingual WER (median ~50% error reduction across ES/FR/DE/IT/PT/JA/KO/ZH/HI/AR) and ~3x lower latency (~626 ms vs ~2300 ms for a typical segment on 8 Gen 3). So the answer to the framing question is yes. But three things change the recommendation. FIRST, the biggest win in this dataset is not the new tier: Qualcomm's own benchmarks show whisper-small — the model we ALREADY ship as multi — runs at ~296 ms/segment on the same NPU, an ~8x speedup at literally zero accuracy risk and zero new download. The NPU port and the turbo upgrade are separable decisions, and the cheap certain one is being skipped for the expensive uncertain one. SECOND, the owner's stated premise is unsupported: the W8A16 quantized variant has NO published benchmarks on any chipset and no published WER — every usable number is from the FLOAT variant. THIRD, the costs are real and mostly unmeasured: per-Hexagon-arch binaries (v75 for 8 Gen 3, not forward compatible, 13 chipset variants), a probable ~800 MB-1 GB asset versus our current 190 MB, a proprietary Qualcomm asset license, no official Android ASR sample, and a fixed 30s encoder window that makes us pay 466 ms even on a 0.3s utterance. Separately, whisper.cpp is a confirmed dead end — the merged ggml-hexagon backend has no convolution ops and therefore structurally cannot run a Whisper encoder, so retiring GGML turbo on CPU stays correct and any NPU tier means maintaining a second inference stack. RECOMMENDED SEQUENCING: Phase 0, download the 8 Gen 3 assets and measure actual size — that is the likeliest deal-breaker and it is unpublished. Phase 1, port the EXISTING small model to NPU; it banks the 8x win and proves the QNN plumbing and per-SoC asset matrix on a model whose accuracy we already trust. Phase 2, add turbo on top reusing that runtime, gated on Qualcomm + Hexagon v75+ + successful binary load with silent fallback to multi, and with Cantonese and Thai explicitly excluded from the tier's advertised languages (turbo is 43.3% CER on Cantonese vs large-v3's 10.5%) and no translation claims (turbo was fine-tuned without translation data). Since multi is already perceived as 'almost instantaneous', sell the tier on accuracy — speed is only a non-regression requirement.

findings.claim: The exact model the owner wants to evaluate benchmarks at 1,421 ms encoder latency on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 — the Z Fold6's own SoC. This is the single decisive number.
findings.detail: From Qualcomm's own raw model card, Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized (w8a16), Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Mobile, all three runtimes: encoder 1421.004 ms (PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX), 1340.577 ms (QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY), 1356.408 ms (VOICE_AI); decoder 4.51 / 4.468 / 4.514 ms per token. This is NOT a Z Fold6 weakness — the encoder is 1232 ms on 8 Elite and 1167/1132 ms on the newest 8 Elite Gen 5, and 2227 ms on 7 Gen 4. The encoder never drops near real-time on any mobile chip. Practical cost per commit on the target device: ~1.34 s (best runtime) + ~4.5 ms/token, so a 10-token utterance is ~1.39 s. Because the input window is fixed (see next finding), a 0.3-second 'yes' costs the same ~1.34 s as a 15-second sentence. Against an owner-perceived 'almost instantaneous' baseline, this is a large regression, not an upgrade tier.

findings.claim: The fixed 30-second input window is hardcoded into the exported graph, which structurally cancels the audio_ctx=512 optimization that made the current multi tier fast.
findings.detail: In qai_hub_models/models/_shared/hf_whisper/model.py: SAMPLE_RATE = 16000, CHUNK_LENGTH = 30, N_SAMPLES = 480000, AUDIO_EMB_LEN = 1500, MELS_AUDIO_LEN = AUDIO_EMB_LEN * 2 (=3000), and the encoder input is declared as shape=(1, num_mel_bins, MELS_AUDIO_LEN). The cross-attention KV cache specs also bind to AUDIO_EMB_LEN. These are module-level constants baked into the TensorSpec at export/quantize/compile time. whisper.cpp's audio_ctx parameter — which the owner already set to 512, cutting encoder work roughly 3x by truncating the 1500-frame audio context — has no equivalent on the QNN path. The app's architecture (segment-per-commit, 0.3–15 s chunks) is exactly the workload this fixed-shape graph handles worst: every short segment is zero-padded to 30 s and pays full encoder cost. The owner's existing optimization and the QNN model are mutually exclusive.

findings.claim: If an NPU tier is pursued at all, Whisper-Small-Quantized is the only defensible candidate — same base checkpoint as the current default, and 5.3x faster on the encoder.
findings.detail: Whisper-Small-Quantized (w8a16) is built from checkpoint openai/whisper-small — the identical multilingual base as the owner's current 'multi' tier (small q5_1). On Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: encoder 270.196 / 270.846 / 268.009 ms across the three runtimes, decoder ~6.0–6.2 ms/token. That is 5.3x faster on the encoder than large-v3-turbo-quantized while being the model class the app already ships. It still pays the fixed 30 s window penalty (~270 ms floor per segment regardless of length), so it is not obviously better than the existing audio_ctx=512 CPU path — but it is the only variant worth measuring. Note the tier the owner proposed would be ABOVE multi; this one is a same-quality-different-runtime swap, which changes the product framing entirely.

findings.claim: The one company that actually shipped Whisper on Qualcomm NPU on Android — in official collaboration with Qualcomm AI Hub — archived the project on 2026-01-24 and moved to Google LiteRT.
findings.detail: argmaxinc/WhisperKitAndroid is confirmed archived:true, pushed 2026-01-24, MIT license, 214 stars. Its README carries an IMPORTANT banner: 'WhisperKitAndroid is deprecated. argmax-sdk-kotlin will soon supplant this repository with an architectural redesign built on top of Google LiteRT.' This was not a hobby project — Qualcomm staff pointed developers to it as the official answer for Android Whisper (ai-hub-models issue #99, comment by mestrona-3 on 2025-01-24: 'We've worked with Argmax to leverage their WhisperKit for Android deployment of Whisper'). This is the strongest available field signal: the best-resourced, Qualcomm-blessed attempt at exactly what the owner is proposing was built, shipped to the Play Store, and then retired.

findings.claim: Argmax's stated reasons for abandoning the Qualcomm-NPU path are directly applicable to this app: single-vendor device coverage and a first-run compilation penalty.
findings.detail: Argmax's own write-up gives two reasons. (1) Device coverage: 'TFLite only supported Qualcomm Snapdragon NPUs,' capping addressable market; LiteRT unified Qualcomm, Google Tensor and MediaTek. (2) Compilation: TFLite lacked ahead-of-time compilation, forcing 'costly on-device just-in-time compilation' that 'severely impacted the first-time user experience.' Their earlier Android post also conceded NPU worked on Samsung Galaxy devices while 'for other Android devices, deployment occurs via GPU as we work toward broad and seamless NPU support.' Caveat worth giving the owner: reason (2) is partly avoidable here, because PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX and QNN_CONTEXT_BINARY assets are pre-compiled per chipset — but that trades the JIT problem for a per-chipset asset matrix (see separate finding). Reason (1) applies fully: an NPU tier is Snapdragon-only in a market where the app currently runs everywhere.

findings.claim: Qualcomm has no first-party Android Whisper sample app. The starting point the owner is imagining does not exist.
findings.detail: Full app listing in qualcomm/ai-hub-apps (repo actively maintained, pushed 2026-08-26, 448 stars): the only Whisper sample is whisper_windows_py — Python, Windows, ONNX, ~12 small files (demo.py is 2,442 bytes; build/install/test are PowerShell). The Android apps are chatapp_android, geniex_chat_android, image_classification_android, object_detection_android, semantic_segmentation_android, super_resolution_android — no ASR among them. The repo README's Android App Directory still lists '[WhisperKit (Speech to Text)](https://github.com/argmaxinc/WhisperKitAndroid)*' — an outbound link to the archived third-party repo, and it is tagged 'TensorFlow Lite', not QNN. So Qualcomm's official Android speech-to-text story is a dead link to a deprecated project. Any Android QNN Whisper integration here is greenfield C++/JNI work against QAIRT, not sample-adaptation.

findings.claim: Sample code license is clean (BSD-3-Clause), but the license for redistributing the model binaries and QNN runtime in a paid app is unresolved and is a genuine blocker to check.
findings.detail: Verified from the repo LICENSE file: qualcomm/ai-hub-apps is BSD-3-Clause, 'Copyright 2025 Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.' — permissive, fine to vendor into a commercial $4.99 app. Separately, the HF model card metadata for both Whisper-Large-V3-Turbo-Quantized and Whisper-Small-Quantized declares license: apache-2.0. However, Qualcomm AI Hub's precompiled .tflite/QNN NPU assets are generally described as released under the Qualcomm AI Model & Software License, and the QAIRT runtime shared objects (libQnnHtp.so and friends) ship under Qualcomm SDK terms of their own. Three different licenses across sample code / model weights / runtime .so, with an apparent conflict on the model layer. For a paid Play Store app this needs explicit legal confirmation before any engineering spend — I could not resolve it from public pages.

findings.claim: Qualcomm's AI Hub product pages for the quantized turbo model contradict the Hugging Face data — the AI Hub page reports the model as unsupported on chipsets while HF publishes full mobile benchmarks.
findings.detail: aihub.qualcomm.com/compute/models/whisper_large_v3_turbo_quantized states verbatim 'This model is currently not supported on any Compute chipset' while simultaneously listing Snapdragon X Elite CRD, X Plus 8-Core CRD and X2 Elite CRD as supported Compute devices. The /mobile/ variant of the URL likewise reported not supported on any Mobile chipset. Meanwhile the HF card publishes complete encoder/decoder tables for 8 Gen 3, 8 Elite, 8 Elite Gen 5, 7 Gen 4 and a dozen Dragonwing parts. Note also that the model is filed primarily under Compute (laptop/X Elite), not Mobile — consistent with the encoder latency profile being tuned for laptop silicon. Read this as a productization-maturity signal: the surface the owner would build a paid feature on is internally inconsistent right now.

findings.claim: Qualcomm claims on-device accuracy within 0.15% of float PyTorch on LibriSpeech — but developers report concrete numerical divergence, and the claim is not specific to the w8a16 turbo model.
findings.detail: Qualcomm engineer 'kory' in ai-hub-models issue #263: 'We have tested end to end accuracy (LibriSpeech) with our whisper model. Accuracy on device is within .15% of floating point accuracy via PyTorch.' Two caveats: it says 'our whisper model' generically, not large-v3-turbo w8a16 specifically; and LibriSpeech is clean read speech, not the noisy real-world dictation this app handles. The reporting user in that same issue found QNN and PyTorch producing different tokens outright (argmax 50260 vs 50359 at the same index) using the official precompiled whisper-small asset; Qualcomm's response was that QAIRT 'may not have bit-exact reimplementations of ops' and 'some small output variance is expected.' Related quantization-pipeline defects: OverflowError during dequantization (ai-hub-models #265, ai-hub-apps #117) and PRECOMPILED_QNN_ONNX runtime failing without AI Hub assets (#242).

findings.claim: No Android dictation app ships NPU-accelerated Whisper today — so 'first' is genuinely available, but the reason it's available is the cautionary part.
findings.detail: Survey of the competitive field: FUTO Voice Input (the leading privacy-focused offline Android voice keyboard) runs whisper.cpp on CPU — same runtime class as this app already uses. Dictate Keyboard (net.devemperor.dictate) is Whisper-based but not NPU-accelerated. Wispr Flow launched Android in Feb 2026 but is cloud-based with a 'Private Mode' toggle, not on-device. The one NPU-accelerated Android entrant, Argmax's WhisperKit Android example app on Google Play, is now backed by an archived repo. Adjacent corroboration that NPU Whisper is not actually reaching users: OpenWhispr issue #867 reports that on Snapdragon X Plus Windows-on-ARM, local Whisper runs entirely on CPU with the Hexagon NPU at 0% utilization. The marketing angle is real but thin: being first at something a well-funded specialist tried and abandoned invites the question of why.

findings.claim: An NPU tier creates a per-chipset binary matrix with a hard device floor at Hexagon v73, narrowing the tier to recent Snapdragon flagships only.
findings.detail: Precompiled assets are published per chipset — separate downloads for 8 Gen 3, 8 Gen 1, 8 Elite, 8 Elite Gen 5, 7 Gen 4, plus Dragonwing/automotive parts — each pinned to specific SDK versions (QAIRT 2.45, ONNX Runtime 1.27.1 for the current release). QNN context binaries are tied to the Hexagon architecture version and QAIRT version they were compiled against, so each Qualcomm SDK bump risks re-validating the whole matrix. Compounding this, ai-hub-models issue #124 establishes that only Hexagon v73 and newer are supported, which excludes older Snapdragons (e.g. SA8295/Hexagon v68). Net effect on the product: the tier would be gated to recent Snapdragon flagships, must ship a chipset-matched binary per device, and would need a maintained CPU fallback for everyone else — meaning the whisper.cpp path stays in the codebase regardless.

findings.claim: Sustained-load thermal behavior on this exact SoC class is a real but secondary risk — roughly 15% throughput degradation, not a cliff.
findings.detail: A 2026 arXiv study of sustained edge inference measured the Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, Adreno 750 — the same SoC as the Z Fold6) degrading '~15% over 20 iterations into a Snapdragon governor-regulated plateau,' versus the iPhone 16 Pro losing 'roughly 40% of its peak throughput within three iterations.' The paper also notes that existing benchmarks including MLPerf 'measure peak performance without tracking thermal throttling or sustained-workload behaviour' — which is precisely what the AI Hub single-shot numbers are. Important honesty caveat: this study measured LLM decode, not Whisper encoder passes, so it is adjacent evidence about the platform's thermal governor rather than a direct measurement of this workload. Treat as a reason to include a sustained-dictation test in any evaluation, not as a standalone blocker. Note that AI Hub's published latencies are best-case single-shot figures and should be discounted for real sustained dictation sessions.

findings.claim: The realistic buy-vs-build alternative is Argmax's commercial LiteRT-based SDK, which is multi-vendor rather than Qualcomm-only.
findings.detail: Argmax Pro SDK 2 is Kotlin-first, built on Google LiteRT, supports both Nvidia Parakeet and OpenAI Whisper for streaming speech-to-text, and Argmax claims to be 'the first commercial SDK to ship with LiteRT that supports virtually all of the major NPU vendors in the Android market' — Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and MediaTek.
